The particle model explains a lot, and this short lesson looks at where it stops working.

## Engage: is the model wrong?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students tend to think a model is either right or wrong; 'useful for some things, not others' is the idea to build."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "The particle model can't explain why copper is orange. What does that mean?"
  options: ["The model has limits: it is still useful for what it does explain", "The model is wrong and should be thrown away", "Copper isn't made of particles", "Colour is not real"]
  actual: "The model has limits. It treats particles as plain balls with no parts, so it can't explain colour. It still explains states, diffusion and pressure very well, so scientists keep using it, alongside other models for other jobs."
```

## Explore: a prediction that works

```step
stage: run
insight: "Testing a prediction the model makes (diffusion, faster in gases) shows what the model is good at before asking what it can't do."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#diffusion", height: 520 }
check: { type: board, text: "Lift the barrier for a gas and for a liquid. Which mixes faster?", expect: { done: true } }
```

## Explain: scope and limits

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Reasoning from what the model assumes (plain moving particles that attract) to what it can and can't explain turns 'limits' into an argument, not a list."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Can the particle model explain it?"
      options: ["Explains it well", "Can't explain it"]
      items:
        - ["A smell spreading across a room", "Explains it well"]
        - ["Air being easy to squash but water not", "Explains it well"]
        - ["A metal bar getting longer when heated", "Explains it well"]
        - ["Why copper is orange and gold is yellow", "Can't explain it", "In the model the particles are plain balls, and plain balls have no colour of their own."]
        - ["Why iron rusts but gold doesn't", "Can't explain it", "Reactions need atoms with parts that can join and swap, and the plain particles in this model don't have any."]
        - ["Why metals conduct electricity", "Can't explain it"]
    hint: ["For each one, ask what the model pictures particles as, and whether the thing needs anything more than that.", "Pick out the ones you can explain by describing how the particles are spaced, how they move or how they attract, and be honest about the ones you can't."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why can't the particle model explain why some substances react?"
      options: ["It treats particles as plain balls with no parts, so it says nothing about how they could join or swap", "Because reactions are too fast to see", "Because the model only works for gases"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Speed isn't what limits the model, so think about what it says a particle is.", "The model works for solids and liquids as well as gases, so that can't be the limit."]
      explain: "To explain a phenomenon, a model needs the right parts. Reactions need atoms that can join and rearrange (Year 8), and electricity needs electrons (Year 9)."
    hint: ["What does the particle model say a particle actually is?", "Now think about what particles would have to be able to do for one substance to turn into a different one, and whether a plain ball can do that."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "What evidence supports the particle model?"
      options: ["Diffusion, gases being compressible, and tiny specks in water jiggling under a microscope", "We can see particles with our eyes", "It explains everything"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Particles are far too small to see with our eyes, so that can't be the evidence.", "No model explains everything, and this one doesn't either."]
      explain: "Tiny grains of pollen in water jiggle (Brownian motion) because moving water particles keep knocking them about, which Einstein explained in 1905 and which is strong evidence for particles."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "The particle model explains a smell spreading across a room. Which part of the model does the explaining?"
      options: ["Particles are always moving, with space between them, so the smell's particles spread out between the air particles", "Smell particles are lighter than air, so they float up and spread", "Smell particles get bigger until they fill the room", "The smell spreads only because a breeze carries it"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Smells spread downwards and sideways as well as up, because the particles move in every direction.", "Particles never change size, so they spread out rather than grow.", "A draught helps, but a smell still spreads in still air, because its particles move by themselves."]
      explain: "The model assumes moving particles with space between them, which is exactly what diffusion needs, so it explains it well."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can name something the particle model explains well and something it can't, with a reason for each." }
```

## Mix it up

```step
stage: practise
insight: "The model is judged by what it explains well. Squashing is a clear case of it working, to set against the cases where it cannot."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Looking back at squashing: a syringe of air can be squashed, but a syringe of water cannot. What does the particle model say is different?"
  options: ["Air particles are far apart, with space to move into; water particles are already close together", "Air particles are smaller than water particles", "Water particles are harder than air particles", "Air has no mass, so nothing pushes back"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Particles of a substance are the same size in every state, so the difference must be something else.", "Particles never squash in any state, so that isn't what makes the difference.", "Air does have mass, about 1.2 g in every litre, so that isn't the reason."]
  explain: "The spacing explains it, and this is the kind of job the particle model does well: explaining how substances behave from the arrangement and motion of their particles."
```

## Elaborate: a better model

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Seeing that the atomic model adds what was missing shows why scientists use several models."
check:
  type: question
  q: "In Year 8 the particles get parts: they are made of atoms of different types that can join. What can this new model explain that the plain particle model couldn't?"
  options: ["Why substances react and make new substances", "Why gases are easy to squash", "Why smells spread"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "The plain particle model already explains that, so it can't be what the new model adds.", "The plain model already explained diffusion, so that isn't something new."]
  explain: "A new model keeps what the old one did well and adds what it couldn't do, and scientists choose the simplest model that does the job."
```

## Elaborate: how the idea grew

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "The long road from an idea to an accepted model shows that evidence, not argument alone, decides."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Ancient Greek thinkers suggested matter is made of tiny particles, but most people didn't accept it for over 2000 years. What changed?"
  options: ["Evidence: experiments on gases, chemical reactions and Brownian motion that the idea explained and predicted", "Someone saw a particle", "It was voted on"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Atoms were first imaged in the 1950s, which was long after the model was accepted, so nobody could have relied on that.", "Science doesn't settle ideas by vote, so that can't be what changed people's minds."]
  explain: "Models are accepted when they explain and predict evidence better than the alternatives, and changed when new evidence doesn't fit."
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my first answer about copper's colour with what I now think about models." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- The particle model says matter is made of tiny particles that move and attract each other.
- It explains states, diffusion, compressing gases and expansion very well, and evidence such as diffusion and Brownian motion supports it.
- It can't explain colour, reactions or electricity, because its particles are plain balls with no parts.
- Every model has a scope and limits. Scientists keep a model for what it does well and use or build other models for the rest.

```teacher
summary: Students identify what the particle model explains well and what it
  can't, reason from its assumptions to its limits, and name evidence for it
  (AC9S7U05, node 5).
time: 15
timing: Engage and Explore 5 min · Explain 7 min · Evaluate 2 min · Typical adds
  1 min, Wider about 1 min
goals:
  - I can name something the particle model explains well, and why.
  - I can name something it can't explain, and why.
  - I can give evidence for the particle model.
before: >
  A short concept tutorial to close the particle theory unit, before Pure
  substance or mixture? Set the width with `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default)
  or `wider`.


  Not a hinge node. The progression asks for reasoning, not a list of limits:
  "what does the model assume, and what does this phenomenon need that the model
  doesn't have?" The sentence starter in "In your own words" scaffolds it.


  Board notes: the diffusion board is the same as in Why can you squash air but
  not water?; here it stands for a prediction the model gets right.
running:
  - "Engage: ask the students who chose 'throw it away' what they would use
    instead for squashing gases."
  - "Explain: the sort is the success criterion; the reactions question is the
    reasoning."
  - "In your own words: one 'explains well' and one 'can't explain', each with a
    reason that starts from the model's assumptions."
struggle: Giving a reason for a limit, not just naming one. When a student
  writes 'it can't explain colour', ask 'what would the particles need to have
  for the model to explain it?'
stuck:
  - see: A student says a model with limits is wrong.
    ask: Is a street map wrong because it doesn't show hills?
    fix: No, it is built for a job. Models are judged by what they explain and
      predict.
  - see: A student lists limits without reasons.
    ask: What does the model say particles are like?
    fix: Plain moving balls that attract. Anything that needs particles to have
      parts (colour, reactions, electricity) is beyond it.
stretch: Particles in a solid are drawn touching, yet solids expand when heated.
  How does the model explain that? (The particles vibrate more and push each
  other slightly further apart.)
support: "Give the sentence frame: 'The model explains … because it says
  particles … . It can't explain … because it says nothing about … .'"
leads: >
  Next: Pure substance or mixture? (AC9S7U06). In Year 8 the particles get parts
  (atoms), which extends the model.


  In class: Brownian motion with smoke in a cell or a video; a class list of
  'explains well' and 'can't explain' to revisit in Year 8.
exit:
  q: Name one thing the particle model explains well and one thing it can't, with
    a reason for each.
  a: "For example: explains diffusion (particles move and mix); can't explain
    colour (particles are plain balls with no parts)."
explain: >
  The particle model treats matter as tiny particles that move and attract each
  other. It explains states, diffusion, compressing gases and expansion very
  well.


  It can't explain colour, reactions or electricity, because its particles have
  no parts. Every model has limits; scientists use the one that suits the job.
```
